lead: Every 8085 instruction runs as a fixed pattern of clock periods on shared bus wires. The timing diagram draws those wires against time, so you can see when the address is valid, when ALE latches it, and when RD or WR moves data. Engineers use it to connect memory and I/O chips, to compute execution time and delays, and to debug a board with a logic analyser. This chapter defines the clock units, shows the five machine cycles, and counts T-states for MVI A, 32H.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for the 8085 registers and the names of its pins and control signals.

blocks.text: A timing diagram plots bus signals against time. The 8085 sends addresses, data and control over shared wires, so the diagram records what each wire carries in each clock period.
A T-state is one period of the CPU clock. A 6 MHz crystal is divided by 2 inside the 8085, giving a 3 MHz CPU clock. One T-state is then 1 ÷ 3,000,000 s = 0.333 µs.

A machine cycle is a group of T-states that completes one bus operation. A memory read takes 3 T-states; a typical opcode fetch takes 4. An instruction cycle is the complete execution of one instruction and contains one or more machine cycles.

The diagram exists because AD7-AD0 is multiplexed. The same eight pins carry the low address byte early in the cycle and data later. ALE says when the address is present. RD or WR says which direction the data moves. A memory chip must obey this order, and a designer reads the diagram to check it.
f<sub>CPU</sub> = f<sub>crystal</sub> ÷ 2;  T = 1 ÷ f<sub>CPU</sub>;  execution time = (number of T-states) × T
blocks.where: f<sub>CPU</sub> is the CPU clock in hertz, f<sub>crystal</sub> is the crystal frequency in hertz, T is one T-state in seconds, and execution time is in seconds.

sections.h3: The five machine cycles and their signals

blocks.text: All five cycles begin with T1 and ALE high. In a memory cycle the CPU puts the high address byte on A15-A8 and the low address byte on AD7-AD0. In an I/O cycle it puts the same 8-bit port address on both A15-A8 and AD7-AD0, and still raises ALE. ALE (address latch enable) is active high for one T-state. It clocks an external latch, usually a 74LS373, which holds the low address while AD7-AD0 later changes to data.
IO/M is low for a memory address and high for an I/O port. RD and WR are active low: the line drawn low is the one doing work.

items: Opcode fetch, 4 T. RD goes low in T2 and T3, the memory places the opcode on AD7-AD0, and the CPU samples it at the end of T3. In T4 the opcode moves to the instruction register and RD returns high.
Memory read, 3 T. Same shape, but data goes to a register, not the instruction register. RD is low in T2 and T3.
Memory write, 3 T. WR is low in T2 and T3, and the CPU drives data out on AD7-AD0. RD stays high.
I/O read, 3 T. IO/M is high, RD is low in T2 and T3. The 8-bit port address appears on both A15-A8 and AD7-AD0.
I/O write, 3 T. IO/M is high, WR is low in T2 and T3, and data goes out on AD7-AD0.

blocks.text: Read any diagram in this order: find the ALE pulses, mark where each machine cycle starts, then check RD, WR and IO/M inside that cycle.

sections.h3: Counting T-states for one-, two- and three-byte instructions

blocks.text: The number of bytes in an instruction suggests its memory accesses, but it does not fix the T-state count. Most one-byte instructions take 4 T, many two-byte instructions 7 T, and many three-byte instructions 10 T. The first byte is always an opcode fetch of 4 T. Each later byte is usually a memory read of 3 T.

Three corrections keep counts honest. (1) Some one-byte instructions take 6, 10 or 12 T for internal work or stack traffic with no operand fetch; use the datasheet value, not the byte rule. (2) An I/O instruction uses an I/O read or write cycle, still 3 T, with IO/M high. (3) Instructions that move data to or from memory or the stack add further machine cycles: LDA 2050H and STA 2050H are 13 T (OF + MR + MR + MR/MW) and CALL 2000H is 18 T (OF + MR + MR + MW + MW).

The figure traces MVI A, 32H. The first four T-states fetch opcode 3EH from 2000H. The next three read 32H from 2001H. ALE pulses in T1 of both cycles, RD is low in T2 and T3 of each cycle, and AD7-AD0 carries address, opcode, address and data in turn.

figure.caption: MVI A, 32H at address 2000H: the opcode fetch takes T1 to T4 and the memory read takes T5 to T7. Notice ALE pulsing once per machine cycle and RD going low only while data is read.

spec.aria: Timing for MVI A, 32H: the opcode fetch uses T1 to T4 and the memory read uses T5 to T7; ALE pulses in T1 and T5, RD is low during T2-T3 and T6-T7, and AD7-AD0 carries address, opcode, address and data in turn.

examples.question: The 8085 instruction MVI A, 32H is stored at address 2000H. Draw the opcode fetch and memory read machine cycles and count the total T-states. A 6 MHz crystal drives the CPU. Find the execution time.
steps: MVI A, 32H is 2 bytes. Its opcode is 3EH at 2000H and its immediate byte is 32H at 2001H.
Machine cycle 1, opcode fetch, 4 T. In T1, A15-A8 = 20H, AD7-AD0 = 00H, ALE = 1, IO/M = 0, RD = 1.
In T2, ALE = 0 and RD = 0; AD7-AD0 becomes an input. In T3 the memory puts 3EH on AD7-AD0 and the CPU samples it.
In T4 the opcode moves to the instruction register and RD returns high. The opcode fetch ends.
Machine cycle 2, memory read, 3 T. In its T1, A15-A8 = 20H, AD7-AD0 = 01H, ALE = 1, RD = 1.
In its T2, ALE = 0 and RD = 0; the memory drives 32H on AD7-AD0. In its T3, 32H is latched into A and RD returns high.
The crystal is 6 MHz, so f<sub>CPU</sub> = 6 ÷ 2 = 3 MHz. T = 1 ÷ 3,000,000 s = 0.333 µs.
examples.answer: A = 32H; the instruction takes 7 T-states, which is 2.333 µs at a 3 MHz CPU clock.
examples.check:
opcode_fetch = 4
memory_read = 3
total = opcode_fetch + memory_read
t_us = total * (1 / 3_000_000) * 1_000_000
print(opcode_fetch)
print(memory_read)
print(total)
print(round(t_us, 3))

traps: ALE is high in T1 of every machine cycle, not only during an opcode fetch. RD goes low only in a read cycle, never in a write.
MVI A, data is 2 bytes, so it needs 4 + 3 = 7 T-states, not 4. The second byte is a memory read, not a second opcode fetch.
RD and WR are active low: a line drawn high is idle. Do not describe the low level as off or inactive.
IO/M high means an I/O port. The 8085 puts an 8-bit port address on both A15-A8 and AD7-AD0; it is not a 16-bit I/O address.
The opcode fetch takes 4 T because T4 transfers the opcode to the instruction register. A memory read needs only 3 T.

quiz.q: Define T-state, machine cycle and instruction cycle.
quiz.a: A T-state is one CPU clock period. A machine cycle is a group of T-states that completes one bus operation. An instruction cycle is the complete execution of one instruction, made of one or more machine cycles.

quiz.q: Which signal latches the low address byte, and what is its active level?
quiz.a: ALE, address latch enable. It is active high and stays high for one T-state in T1 of each machine cycle.

quiz.q: Why is ALE needed when AD7-AD0 is multiplexed?
quiz.a: AD7-AD0 carries the low address byte in T1 and data later. ALE clocks an external latch in T1 so the low address is held steady while the same pins switch to data.

quiz.q: MVI B, 0FH is stored at 3000H and the CPU clock is 3 MHz. How many T-states and how much time does it take?
quiz.a: It is a 2-byte instruction: opcode fetch 4 T plus memory read 3 T = 7 T. T = 0.333 µs, so time = 7 × 0.333 µs = 2.333 µs.

quiz.q: A timing diagram shows ALE high in T1 and T5, and RD low in T2-T3 and T6-T7. Which machine cycles are these and how many bytes is the instruction?
quiz.a: The first is a 4 T opcode fetch and the second is a 3 T memory read, giving 7 T total. The instruction is 2 bytes long.

quiz.q: List the signal states in an 8085 I/O write machine cycle.
quiz.a: T1: port address on A15-A8 and AD7-AD0, ALE high, IO/M high, WR high. T2 and T3: ALE low, WR low, data on AD7-AD0. At the end of T3, WR returns high.

quiz.q: Why does an opcode fetch take 4 T-states while a memory read takes 3?
quiz.a: Both put out an address in T1 and read data in T2-T3. The opcode fetch has an extra T4 in which the opcode is moved to the instruction register and decoded, so it needs one more T-state.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern processors replace these visible bus cycles with bursts and cache line fills, but the same idea survives in SDRAM timing: setup, access and hold windows. Datasheets still publish timing diagrams with minimum and maximum nanoseconds, and wait states are added when a slow memory or peripheral cannot meet them. A logic analyser capture of ALE, RD and the address lines is the standard way to debug a stubborn 8085 board. Search for 8085 timing diagram, ALE 74LS373 latch and wait state generation next.
